paragraphs: President Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller, currently deputy chief of staff, will become White House chief of staff on Monday, replacing Susie Wiles. NPR and Fox News both reported the announcement, which Trump made on social media. According to Fox News, Trump said Wiles will move to his political operation.

Trump called Miller one of his "most trusted advisors" and wrote of Wiles, "She has done a great job!" Wiles said in a statement, "Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff," and called serving Trump "the honor of a lifetime." A White House official told Fox News Digital the decision was "very amicable" and that Wiles handed in her resignation Thursday night.

The change comes after Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate in this week's midterm elections. Fox News said the war with Iran and affordability concerns loomed over the vote. NPR described Miller as a fixture in Trump's circles since 2016 and an architect of some of his core policies, including immigration.

Fox News said Wiles has served 21 months, making her Trump's longest-serving chief of staff across both terms; John Kelly served about 17 months in the first term. Fox also noted that she faced scrutiny over a Signal group chat and a December 2025 Vanity Fair interview. Wiles said earlier this year she had early-stage breast cancer and announced in September that she was cancer free.

Vice President Vance, communications director Steven Cheung and Attorney General Todd Blanche posted praise for both Wiles and Miller, according to Fox News. The pages did not include reaction from Democrats.

U.S. employers added a seasonally adjusted 165,000 jobs in October, well above the 59,000 forecast in a Dow Jones estimate, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday, according to CNBC. The unemployment rate edged down to 4.1%, against a forecast of 4.2%.

Earlier months were revised up. August moved to 186,000 and September to 60,000. Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% on the month and 3.1% from a year earlier, above estimates of 0.3% and 2.9%. Hiring was broader than recent trends, CNBC said: professional and business services added 70,000 jobs, healthcare 42,000, transportation and warehousing 25,000 and manufacturing 19,000.

Economists welcomed the report. Dan North of Allianz Trade called it "a really, really good report," and Heather Long of Navy Federal Credit Union said the market is on "much better footing than a year ago." Not every measure improved. A broader unemployment gauge rose 0.3 percentage point to 7.9%, as the labor force grew by 421,000. The average duration of unemployment rose to 27.1 weeks, the highest since September 2021.

For the Federal Reserve, the data arrives as officials weigh whether to resume raising rates at their Dec. 8-9 meeting, with inflation above the 2% target. According to CME Group's FedWatch tool, traders put the odds of a quarter-point hike at 76.8%. Treasury yields rose, while stock futures were mixed.
What to watch: the December Fed decision, and whether hiring stays broad after healthcare drove most gains last year, as Long noted.

The average jobless American has now been out of work for more than 27 weeks, according to the October jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. CNBC reported that this is nearly seven months of searching, the longest outside the pandemic period since 2016.

About 2 million people have been unemployed for at least 27 weeks. These long-term unemployed made up 27.6% of all jobless workers in October, the highest share since late 2021. Cory Stahle, senior economist at Indeed, said the series can be noisy month to month, but over a longer period "there is no mistake in the trend."

CNBC linked the pattern to a "low-hire, low-fire" market in which companies are reluctant to cut workers but also hesitant to add them. Research cited in the article says long-term unemployment is associated with depleted savings, lower future earnings and declining mental health. Researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond wrote earlier this year that time spent unemployed may itself reduce the chance of finding work.

Stahle said most unemployment benefits end after 26 weeks, so the typical jobless worker now takes longer to find a job than benefits last. CNBC said that may partly explain why jobless claims have stayed low.

The trend contrasts with other data. Payrolls rose 165,000 in October, the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, and a separate report showed job openings above forecasts and layoffs at their lowest in over a year. CNBC also noted planned job cuts at Disney and a 5% headcount reduction at American Express.

Asian and European stock markets fell Friday after a technology sell-off on Wall Street a day earlier, according to The Guardian and CNBC. The Nasdaq sank 5.5% Thursday, its worst day in 19 months, and closed more than 10% below its recent peak. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.2%.

In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped about 6% and South Korea's Kospi fell more than 6.5%, The Guardian reported. CNBC said SK Hynix lost 10.44%, Samsung Electronics 6.35%, SoftBank Group 10.83% and TSMC 4.69%. In Europe, the FTSE 100 fell as much as 2.35% but closed down 1%, and Germany's Dax lost 2%. CNBC said European tech was among the least affected sectors, with ASML and ASMI rising.

CNBC reported that investors worried the Democrats' midterm victory could bring tighter limits on data center development, which could slow demand for AI chips. Goldman Sachs strategist Timothy Moe said potential political opposition to U.S. data center construction may affect Asian suppliers, adding that unwinding of positions and stop-loss selling worsened the fall.

Opinions on what comes next differed. IG analyst Chris Beauchamp warned there is a risk of "much more selling to come." Mohit Kumar of Jefferies said he did not see the start of an unwind of the AI trade, arguing that Democrats were unlikely to give up on a growth engine that creates jobs.
U.S. stocks recovered part of Thursday's losses on Friday after a strong jobs report. Most major indices remain up for the year, The Guardian noted, with the Nasdaq Composite up 6.35% in 2026.

Microsoft is reducing the number of neocloud partners it uses, according to CNBC, which cited people familiar with the matter. Those sources said the company is focusing on a few key suppliers and on building out its own data centers. Bloomberg reported the plans earlier.

The sources said Microsoft is still evaluating and has not decided which neoclouds it will stop using. Two people said Microsoft chose not to renew a deal with Oracle. A Microsoft spokesperson said its strategy is "built on flexibility and choice," combining owned, leased and partner capacity, and that it regularly reviews investments against customer demand.

Microsoft's neocloud partners include CoreWeave, Nebius, Chronoscale, IREN, Lambda and Nscale. CNBC said Microsoft has already scaled back with Nscale, walking away from a site in England, which a Microsoft executive tied to electricity access. The Financial Times reported that it also declined to renew an Nscale contract in Texas.

The neocloud sector is under strain, CNBC said, from rising borrowing costs, heavy debt and doubts about how long the buildout will last. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are down roughly half over the past month even after Friday's rally. IREN said it delivered data center capacity to Microsoft in August, but a requested networking upgrade pushes it online to January or February. IREN's co-CEO said markets have shifted to asking whether contracts can be delivered, financed and run at a profit.
CoreWeave and Nebius report quarterly results next week. CoreWeave said last year that 62% of its 2024 revenue came from Microsoft.

OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar said Friday that the company will keep investing in AI infrastructure despite voter opposition to data centers in Tuesday's midterm elections. She spoke to CNBC at the Citi TMT Leadership Summit in California. "I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand," she said, adding that this means continuing to raise capital.

CNBC reported that of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one, according to Ballotpedia and CNBC's own results. Friar said she does not think the election changed much for OpenAI. The company published a policy blueprint Thursday with commitments for its own future data centers. "We will never raise your electricity bill," she said.

Investors have grown wary of AI stocks over higher borrowing costs, debt and public backlash. The Nasdaq fell sharply Thursday and rebounded partly Friday. Other executives interviewed by CNBC were more upbeat. Arm CEO Rene Haas called the post-election fear "very, very short term thinking," and said that if the U.S. hesitates, other countries are ready to build. Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said data centers are only one segment of his business.

On OpenAI's plans, Friar said the company confidentially filed for an IPO in June and is still looking at a 2027 debut, while rival Anthropic aims to list in mid-November. She said OpenAI is in talks to raise funding and that the round is ongoing.

Activists broke into the construction site of a Microsoft data center in Amsterdam on Friday, The Guardian reported. Members of the Dutch direct action group Geef Tegengas clashed with police at the Westpoort site, climbing a crane, lighting flares and tying helium balloons to equipment. They hung banners objecting to Microsoft's services to the Israeli military and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Police told Dutch broadcaster NOS they tried to stop the occupation but could not, that force was used, and that one officer was slightly injured. Protesters from both groups said police used force and teargas.

The break-in was separate from a Europe-wide "Stop Dirty Data Centres" campaign, whose members stayed outside the fence. That coalition, which includes national branches of Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth, said it had not coordinated the direct action but called it "understandable" when communities feel shut out of decisions. More than 100 groups are involved in two days of protests demanding moratoria on new data centers, with smaller events in Bristol, Berlin, Warsaw and Zagreb. More are expected Saturday.

Geef Tegengas activist Roos Molenaar said the data center is "gulping up our drinking water." Microsoft said it respects peaceful expression but does not condone unlawful actions or those that risk safety. Site owner Pure Data Centres said entering a live construction site was unlawful and dangerous and asked protesters to leave and talk.
The Guardian said governments across Europe have backed data center building to raise revenue and keep pace with the U.S. and China.

Several incoming Democratic senators have declined to back Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader, The Guardian reported, though it said he likely still has enough votes to keep the job. As of Friday afternoon he was running uncontested, with no other Senate Democrat having entered the race.

Annie Andrews, senator-elect from South Carolina, told Fox News it is "time for generational change on both sides of the aisle." Adam Hamilton of Kansas told CNN he would not support Schumer. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan declined again to back him and said he wanted to consider other options. The Guardian said others who have not committed include James Talarico, Juliana Stratton, Chris Pappas, Peggy Flanagan and Troy Jackson.
Schumer, 75, has led Senate Democrats since 2017. He told reporters, "I'll be re-elected as majority leader," and said, "The issue is not me," adding that the focus should be on what Americans want.

Fox News reported a separate source of friction: a feud between Sen. John Fetterman and El-Sayed over Israel aid, Medicare for All and the party's direction. El-Sayed has said his campaign appearances and positions reflect his opposition to military aid, while Fetterman has criticized him sharply; the feud was described as a possible test of Schumer's push for unity. Fox said El-Sayed, Fetterman and Schumer did not respond to its requests for comment. A longtime Democratic staffer told Fox that party loyalty would likely outweigh personal disagreements.

South Africa's ruling African National Congress is heading for a heavy loss in Wednesday's local elections, according to The Guardian. With more than 80% of ballots counted, the party had 31.8% of the national vote, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local result. The centre-right Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1%, and the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of former president Jacob Zuma had 9.3%.

The Guardian said the fragmented result marks another stage in the ANC's decline since it began leading national governments in 1994, and cited high unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery. The party is projected to lose its place as the biggest party in Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal. The election commission estimated turnout at 54.5%, up from 46% five years ago.

In Johannesburg, with just over half of votes counted, the DA led with 40%, the ANC had 17.5% and ActionSA had 15.5%. The city has had 10 mayors in a decade and has admitted to a 220bn rand infrastructure spending backlog. ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba has pledged never to work with the DA's Helen Zille, whom he calls racist; she denies this. Many ANC township strongholds had not yet reported. The research body CSIR projects the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.

In KwaZulu-Natal, MK is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party. In eThekwini, which contains Durban, MK had 41% with half the votes counted, so other parties could form a coalition to keep it out. The DA is projected to keep its majority in Cape Town.
Final results are expected on Sunday. Parties have begun coalition talks behind closed doors, and councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

Paraguay's Senate convened a rare session on Friday to consider the political future of President Santiago Peña, moving ahead with impeachment even though he announced his resignation on Thursday, according to Al Jazeera and The Guardian. Peña has requested a 72-hour extension to prepare his defence.

The crisis centres on Ueno Bank, a fast-growing digital lender. The central bank ordered it into resolution over insolvency last Monday, freezing deposits for about 3 million customers. Al Jazeera reported that the collapse left more than half the population without access to accounts. Ueno held between $800m and $850m in state and pension funds. Executives were arrested, and thousands of people protested outside Congress.

Lawmakers accuse Peña of misconduct and a conflict of interest. He held a stake in Ueno's parent group until last year, and says he sold his shares. The Guardian reported he called press reports of favouritism a "false media campaign" and has insisted he did nothing wrong. Opposition senator Rafael Filizzola called the case "the biggest fraud carried out from political power in the democratic era." In a video, Peña apologised and said he wanted deposits returned.

The lower house approved the impeachment motion unanimously, which Al Jazeera put at 78-0. Former president Horacio Cartes, a former ally, endorsed it. The central bank chief resigned, and the attorney general ordered three criminal investigations.

The Guardian noted that Congress must in theory accept the resignation, after which Vice President Pedro Alliana would take over. Alliana has denied suspicion of involvement in the scandal. If the Senate convicts Peña, he would lose his Senate seat and immunity, leaving him open to prosecution in ordinary courts.

Taiwan says it is closing its representative office in Papua New Guinea and will stop buying liquefied natural gas from the country, blaming Chinese political pressure. Taiwan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday that Papua New Guinea had repeated earlier demands that staff leave the office in Port Moresby within a set deadline and had pushed for its closure.

In a statement, the ministry said the actions "reflect China's continued use of political pressure and economic influence to interfere in other countries' diplomatic decisions and suppress Taiwan's international space." China, which claims Taiwan as part of its territory, had welcomed Papua New Guinea's decision in July to shut the office. Taipei rejected that move, and the office stayed open in the meantime. Papua New Guinea has formal diplomatic relations with China but had allowed Taiwan a representative office.

Taiwan had earlier announced it had stopped spot purchases of LNG from the country. On Friday the ministry said it also would no longer sign new spot purchase contracts. Al Jazeera reported that Taiwanese purchases accounted for one-third of Papua New Guinea's exports, while Taiwan imported about 8 percent of its natural gas from Port Moresby last year.
Taipei will also end technical cooperation and assistance programmes, including medical missions, scholarships and talent development programmes, the ministry said.

The Pacific has long been an arena of diplomatic competition between Beijing and Taipei. Taiwan has formal ties with only three Pacific Islands nations: Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands. It also has a representative office in Fiji, and just 12 countries worldwide maintain formal diplomatic ties with it. China's response to the latest announcement was not included in the report.

Free, downloadable AI models are now nearly as capable of hacking computer networks as the best closed models, according to new research from Vals, a company that measures AI capabilities, as reported by Wired. Vals tested how well different models could carry out complex, multi-step instructions on mock corporate networks.

OpenAI's most advanced cyber model, Daybreak, which is available only to trusted partners, was the most capable, completing 81 percent of its tasks on average across two tests. The Chinese open-weight model DeepSeek completed 73 percent. Vals said the two scored equally on some tasks. Open models were also far cheaper to use: Vals put the token cost of an attack with GPT-6-Sol at $17 to $46, against $2 to $3 for DeepSeek. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Wired said the findings suggest closed models no longer hold a clear edge in cyber skills, which could undercut efforts by US labs to limit access. Anthropic limited the release of its Claude Mythos Preview in April on the premise that gated access would only buy time. Anthropic's Logan Graham told Wired then that the company expected such capabilities to be broadly available in 6, 12 or 24 months.

Wired noted caveats. Experts still debate whether AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity or amplified existing problems. Observers have found attackers mostly use older, less capable models. Alex Zenla of the security firm Edera said closed labs have probably trained unreleased models that go further, and described the situation as a cat-and-mouse game that may be the start of a dangerous security landscape.

Health ISAC, the information-sharing group for the healthcare industry, has warned members about a wave of cyberattacks on refrigeration controllers, including one that affected a major French blood bank, according to a bulletin seen by NPR. The bulletin was issued for situational awareness and describes attacks on specific refrigeration brands.

The French Blood Establishment said in a Tuesday press release that a vendor used in its cold storage rooms was targeted, causing defrost and temperature thresholds to be raised dangerously high. It detected the suspicious activity in time to rescue blood samples. Errol Weiss, Health ISAC's chief security officer, told NPR that such attacks directly endanger the physical resources needed to sustain life.

On Thursday, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI, the Department of Health and Human Services and the Department of Agriculture published a fact sheet on threats to industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems. The FBI's Brett Leatherman said the bureau is tracking bad actors targeting these systems across critical infrastructure sectors globally.

It remains unclear who is responsible, or whether multiple groups are involved. Iran has been linked to one incident in Israel earlier in the spring, and investigators are considering it as a possible culprit in disruptions at US military bases. Two pro-Russian groups, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance, claimed the European attacks, but some experts are skeptical. SentinelOne's Tom Hegel said more evidence, such as access logs and configuration changes, is needed, and that such groups often claim incidents even when the claims are false.
NPR reported that thousands of refrigeration controllers in France were exposed to the open internet with almost no protection before the October attacks, and hundreds remained unprotected afterward.

Companies are using more AI but not spending more on it, according to a new report from Ramp covered by TechCrunch. Ramp's data shows token spending grew only 1.5% across August and September, compared with 42% growth in July alone, even as token volumes rose. The report comes as Anthropic prepares for an IPO.

Ramp lead economist Ara Kharazian said almost all AI spending comes from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies, and that if they slow down together there could be cascading effects. He said the top 1% of firms, the most heavily AI-focused, stuttered slightly, landing just below the $10,000 per employee they hit at their summer peaks. Median firms spend $12 to $15 per employee per month and the top 10% spend $600 to $1,000. Spending among those groups grew, but not enough to offset the top 1%.

Kharazian attributed the stall to competition rather than weak demand. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Anthropic also cut prices for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, which the company said in a filing reduced revenue growth by about $600 million. Kharazian also pointed to cheaper models from Meta, Nvidia and open-model companies, and to customers getting better at controlling costs through budgets, defaults and routers.

October data showed a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, though Kharazian said headwinds remain strong. Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic's potential valuation fell from an estimated $2 trillion in early October to $1.2 to $1.3 trillion, and that OpenAI lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion. Investors are hoping a new breakthrough use case will drive further spending.

The European Commission has issued a preliminary ruling charging TikTok with failing to protect users' mental health, according to The Guardian. The regulator said the platform's algorithm "can be harmful" and was leading young and vulnerable users "down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from." TikTok has 189 million users in the EU.

The investigation focused on legal content, where a single video may be harmless but watching many on one theme, such as body image or isolation, could worsen anxiety or eating disorders. Officials said TikTok's safeguards were ineffective. For example, pressing "not interested" on a video about eating patterns still produced similar diet and body-image content, and refreshing a feed brought only brief respite. Henna Virkkunen, the Commission's lead official on tech policy, said TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect wellbeing, including that of minors.

TikTok said the Commission made statements that are "fundamentally inaccurate" and distort its platform's architecture. It said its policies prohibit content promoting disordered eating and that more than 79 million EU users used its "not interested" or keyword filters in the first half of 2026. The Molly Rose Foundation welcomed the findings and urged the UK regulator Ofcom to open its own investigation.

The findings are part of an inquiry launched in February 2024 under the Digital Services Act. The Commission previously found TikTok violated EU rules over "addictive design" features such as infinite scroll, which the company called meritless and said it would challenge.

TikTok can now examine the investigation file and mount a defence. It could agree to change its recommender system to avoid a fine. If officials uphold the finding, the company could face a fine of up to 6% of its global turnover. Officials want changes to the ForYou feed to give users more control.

The Senate could vote as early as next week to advance a large bipartisan energy permitting bill, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center, as reported by The Verge. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act was introduced on September 30 by Republican Senators Shelley Moore Capito and Mike Lee and Democratic Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich.

Supporters say it would speed up energy projects and could lower utility bills. Whitehouse said it would help "flood the grid with clean, affordable energy" and make data centers pay their fair share. Climate and renewable groups backed it, and so did fossil fuel interests; the US Oil & Gas Association urged lawmakers to pass it. Xan Fishman of the Bipartisan Policy Center called it a good bipartisan compromise and said lengthy litigation has slowed projects of all kinds.

The bill would set a 45-day deadline for a lead agency to decide on a project after completing a National Environmental Policy Act review. It would narrow which projects require that review, set a 150-day limit for court challenges under several environmental laws, and bar courts from halting a project even if an agency violated the act, instead requiring the agency to fix the problems.

Critics worry about the trade-offs. Christy Goldfuss of the Natural Resources Defense Council said data centers would not have to answer to local communities' concerns, and that people would be shocked at how quickly lawmakers are moving.

Timing is uncertain. Fishman expects President Trump to want to sign the bill if the current Republican-controlled Congress acts. After the midterm elections, however, Democrats could drag out debate until next year to win more concessions, according to The Verge.

Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth next week, according to Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram. Under House rules, Fox reports, the chamber must consider them within two days.

Massie tried before the midterms. Fox reports that the House adjourned a day early in September, which ended his effort and let the articles expire. Speaker Mike Johnson condemned Massie's push but insisted he had not sent members home early out of fear that the House had the votes to impeach.

Fox says the House could move to table the articles or send them to committee, but a growing number of House Republicans have grumbled about Hegseth, so dismissal might not work. Its analysis is that all Democrats are likely to vote to impeach, some Republicans have said privately they would like to, and absences among members who lost could change the count. A simple majority is needed to impeach. Conviction in the Senate requires two-thirds, and Fox notes the Senate could dismiss articles by simple majority, as it did with those against former Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas.

On NPR's Morning Edition, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called Hegseth "the most unqualified secretary of defense in American history." Asked whether he should be impeached, Jeffries said, "I don't want to get out ahead of the caucus," and added, "He's got to go." NPR reports that Massie has threatened to force a vote on eight articles unless Hegseth resigns.

In a video, Hegseth described the push as political theater and said, "Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me." The articles' fate will become clearer once Massie files them next week.

A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of President Donald Trump's planned 250-foot "triumphal arch" in Washington, according to the BBC. US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ordered a 14-day pause before any work can start. The Trump administration had said construction could begin this week.

The order followed a vote earlier on Thursday by the National Capital Planning Commission, which approved the project 8-4 after nearly nine hours of public comment. The White House commended the decision. After the court order, a spokesperson criticized the judge's court as an "activist district court" and said the administration was "confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."

Commission chairman Mark Paoletta, a Trump appointee, said the president understands "it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments." He and other commissioners said the arch fulfills a 100-year plan for a monumental work on Columbia Island and would give Arlington National Cemetery "the monumental gateway it deserves."

Opponents disagree. Democratic Rep. Jared Huffman told the commission the arch would disrupt sightlines of both Arlington and the Lincoln Memorial, and called it "a tribute to Donald Trump." Veterans quoted by the BBC said it would lessen the solemn nature of a cemetery visit, and two said they would try to impede construction workers.

The BBC reports that several lawsuits raise concerns about the environment, traffic congestion and safety, and that there is a dispute over whether congressional approval is needed. It is not yet clear when construction could begin. The arch is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary, and the administration has also said it would double as a complex for storing military equipment.

Houston Mayor John Whitmire said on Friday that the city will limit its cooperation with federal immigration authorities, describing "a new model" of enforcement, according to The Guardian. The announcement came after Democrats won Texas's governor's race for the first time in decades.

Whitmire said the city would focus on immigrants "that pose a danger, not those that are going about their family business, work and education." For a traffic incident, he said, police would write a citation or a warning, with "no contact with ICE over nonviolent, non-jailable offenses."

Under the two-page directive, Houston police should contact ICE only if a person is arrested on a charge that carries jail time or if ICE issues an administrative warrant. The order says that being, or being suspected to be, subject to immigration enforcement is not by itself a basis to contact ICE or prolong a detention. ICE spokespersons did not immediately respond to a request for comment, The Guardian reports.

The paper links the move to recent events in Houston. In July, ICE agents shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during a traffic stop while reportedly looking for other people. In October, a grand jury indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales for aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after a pursuit in which Miguel Parra Hernandez's leg was broken. Prosecutors say video contradicts ICE's account that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle.

The Guardian notes that ICE depends heavily on local police and has signed about 2,600 agreements deputizing local agencies, many in Texas. Outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott, who lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, had aligned the state with the Trump administration on enforcement. Cesar Espinosa of the group Fiel Houston said, "Today Houston won."

Tesla CEO Elon Musk said on Friday that the company will "be winding down" Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of next year, according to CNBC. In a post on X, Musk said ending production would make room for the Cybercab, the company's two-seat robotaxi.

The Cybertruck is built only at the Texas plant, alongside the Model Y and the Cybercab. Musk did not say whether it would be made elsewhere. Responding to a user on X, he said the truck was the best vehicle Tesla has made but that "the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time." Tesla did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

Sales fell well short of Musk's pre-launch prediction of 250,000 a year. Cox Automotive estimated U.S. sales last year at 20,237, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. TechCrunch reports that the base price rose to around $60,000 from a promised figure under $40,000, and that range fell short of the 500 miles Tesla first advertised. According to CNBC, the truck had 11 voluntary recalls for the 2024 model year, covering issues from a "trapped" accelerator pedal risk to software defects and an inverter fault.
Both outlets say the truck's image was affected after Musk became a major backer of Donald Trump and led the Department of Government Efficiency, with some owners reporting harassment.

TechCrunch says Tesla is shifting toward AI and robotics. It has put Cybercabs on Austin streets for two months and plans to expand to Dallas later this month. Earlier this year, the company ended the Model S and Model X to make room for Optimus humanoid robots.

A new wave of bomb threats disrupted air traffic across Europe on Friday, but the affected aircraft landed safely and searches found no explosives, according to The Guardian. At least 18 flights to or from Bulgaria, Cyprus, Czechia, France, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Romania and the UK were affected. Hungary scrambled fighter jets three times to escort civilian flights, its defense minister said. Eurocontrol data cited by the paper puts the affected flights at 0.0674% of those scheduled.

Threats on Tuesday and Thursday had already forced at least 35 flights to be diverted or searched. On Friday, media organizations in Ireland also received threats, prompting evacuations, police searches and disrupted broadcasts. Sky in the UK reported a security threat. The Irish government suggested a "co-ordinated campaign of disruption," the BBC reports.

Some Thursday threats were signed "fighters of the Male State," a reference to a Russian far-right, misogynistic movement. Its founder, Vladislav Pozdniakov, denied involvement on Telegram and said the group has not existed since 2021. Italy's La Stampa nonetheless suggested the group was behind the threats. The Guardian says investigators have seen no evidence that a hostile state or terror group is orchestrating the hoaxes, but inquiries continue.

Officials differ in emphasis. Spain's foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, called a "hybrid aggression" the most reasonable assumption, while Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said it was unclear whether the hoaxes and recent cyber-attacks were connected. London police chief Mark Rowley urged authorities not to "overreact to every message we get online." A senior NATO military official said the alliance was monitoring the situation.

Russia's battlefield gains in Ukraine have fallen to almost nothing this year, according to figures from the Institute for the Study of War and Kyiv's military, as reported by Al Jazeera. The ISW counts 117.38 square kilometers seized in the first 10 months of 2026, compared with 5,304 in 2025 and 3,604 in 2024. Ukraine's General Staff estimates 381,300 Russian personnel killed or seriously wounded from January to October. Al Jazeera could not independently verify casualty claims by either side.

Zelenskyy and his prime minister cite these trends as a reason Russia is intensifying long-range strikes on energy infrastructure. Al Jazeera reports that Russia fired 2,346 drones and more than 80 missiles in the week ending November 6. Ukraine says at least 50 people died in an attack on the village of Komyshuvakha.

On oil, Ukraine hit eight Russian refineries in seven days. Al Jazeera says the strikes aim to cut Russian export revenue and undermine an October 9 arrangement in which Trump invited Russia to sell 1.8 million tonnes of diesel to the global market. The Financial Times reported that four Russian diesel tankers have failed to find buyers willing to risk legal consequences. The Kremlin dismissed that report as fake news. Sen. Richard Blumenthal warned a shipping company that only Congress can make such a transaction legally valid.

Separately, Ukrainian military intelligence told Reuters that Russia is already using its new Rassvet satellite network, billed as a homegrown Starlink, for military communications over Ukraine. It said 32 satellites have been launched this year, with coverage that is currently intermittent. Russia's defense ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters.

Russia supported Iran's military buildup more than previously disclosed, according to a Fox News report based on internal Russian defense industry documents. The documents were obtained and published by Dallas Analytics, a Ukrainian defense intelligence research group. Fox has not independently confirmed them in the article.

The records show components allocated for 90 APU-L twin-rail launchers under a contract labeled "K-10," with shipments within the Russian production chain scheduled from late 2024 through December 2025. Other documents identify K-10 as Iran, including an October 2022 supply request listing the consignee as "K10 Iran." Dallas Analytics also said the tail number of an Iranian Yak-130 matched a number listed for K-10 in Russian factory records. The launchers are designed to carry the LMUR guided missile, also known as the Kh-39.
Fox notes the documents do not establish whether the completed launchers reached Iran. Dallas Analytics told the outlet the contract is "a very strong proof" of a transfer.

The report says President Donald Trump has downplayed Russia's role, saying last month he did not believe Moscow is helping Iran "at all." Fox cites reports that U.S. intelligence assessed Russia gave Iran information on American military locations, and more recently satellite imagery and weapons components. Administration officials have said the support has not materially affected the U.S. campaign. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it was not impeding operations, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the U.S. was tracking it and accounting for it in battle plans.

Fox says it asked the White House, State Department and Pentagon for comment. The State Department this week sanctioned a Russia-based individual accused of helping Iran buy Chinese-made portable air-defense systems.

Armed men believed to be linked to an ISIL-affiliated group raided villages in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo overnight, killing at least 33 people, according to authorities and civil society groups cited by Al Jazeera. The attack hit Cantine, about 50 kilometers west of Beni in North Kivu province.

Beni territorial administrator Colonel Charles Omeonga told Reuters that fighters from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) set fire to houses and killed civilians. Local civil society leader Justin Paluku told the AP that 33 bodies had been counted and more than 50 houses burned. Another local leader, Tchetche Aliamini, said most victims had gunshot wounds, while others were burned or hacked with machetes.

The attackers also burned a health post, forcing patients with confirmed and suspected Ebola to flee. Christian Kakule, medical director of the Kelekele Hospital Centre, said 180 patients left, including one confirmed Ebola case, and that high-risk contacts under monitoring also fled. He warned that probable cases moving about in the open could become a source of transmission.

The violence comes as the country faces what Al Jazeera calls the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak in history. North Kivu accounts for almost half of new infections in the Bundibugyo outbreak, and Africa CDC has recorded more than 10,000 cases and 5,300 deaths nationwide.

The ADF has roots in Uganda and pledged allegiance to ISIL in 2019. In July 2025, it killed 66 people in eastern Congo, in what the UN called a "bloodbath." Paluku called the latest attack "a major security failure" given the number of security forces deployed nearby. The report does not include a response from the government or military.

A Kenyan court in Mombasa has sentenced Paul Mackenzie, leader of the Good News International church, to 200 years in prison over the Shakahola forest deaths. The Guardian describes the victims as 190 children and one adult, while the BBC reports 191 people, all but one of them children. Both say the sentence came after his conviction on October 19.

Prosecutors said Mackenzie ran a doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to reach heaven before the world ended. The BBC reports he was sentenced to 100 years for homicide and 100 years for starvation-related offenses. Sentences within each category run concurrently, but the two sets run consecutively. Justice Diana Mochache said he bore "primary criminal culpability."

Prosecutors had sought the death penalty. The judge said the case met the threshold but declined to impose it, saying capital punishment would eliminate any prospect of rehabilitation. The BBC notes Kenya has not carried out an execution since 1987. Twenty-eight co-accused, including guards and gravediggers, received sentences of up to 160 years. Mackenzie denied forcing anyone to starve, and he and his co-accused asked for leniency.

More than 400 bodies have been recovered from the forest, but the judgment covered 191 deaths, with investigations into more than 200 others continuing, according to The Guardian. Mackenzie also faces other charges, including terrorism, which he denies. Prosecutors say he directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village while in detention, and he has pleaded not guilty. The case has prompted calls for tougher oversight of religious organizations, and a Kenyan rights commission found officials had repeatedly ignored the cult's activities, the BBC reports.

Nigeria's Federal High Court has removed the leadership of the opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC) and ruled that the nomination of its presidential candidate, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, is invalid, the BBC reports. Presidential elections are scheduled for January 16. President Bola Tinubu's main challengers are expected to be Abubakar and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi.

The case was brought by Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former ADC deputy national chairman. He argued that David Mark's takeover as interim chairman was unlawful because Mark was not elected at a national convention, and that he himself should have led the party after the former chairman resigned in 2025. In July, a different judge, Musa Liman, found that Mark had been chosen in accordance with the law and the party constitution in a case brought by another former member. Abubakar asked why another case was filed to reopen the dispute.

The ADC called Thursday's ruling by Justice Peter Lifu "a calculated attempt to weaken the ADC and frustrate" Abubakar's candidacy, and said it will appeal. Abubakar, 79, wrote that he is staying in the race: "We will be on the ballot." The BBC notes that the electoral commission has already issued its final candidate list, which includes Abubakar with Rotimi Amaechi as running mate. The ruling's reasoning beyond the points reported was not detailed in the article, and no response from the APC or the court was included.

Obi, now running for the Nigeria Democratic Congress, said he was shocked and that three months before a general election, certainty is in the public interest. The BBC says the dispute could create uncertainty for hundreds of ADC candidates and raise questions over who can represent them.

An infant in Wisconsin has died of measles, the state's first measles death since 1990, officials reported Thursday, according to Ars Technica. The state's outbreak has sickened more than 430 people across 13 counties this year. Health Secretary Kirsten Johnson said any death of a child is a tragedy, "and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease."

It is the third US measles death reported this week, after a New York child on Monday and a Pennsylvania death on Wednesday. Ars Technica counts nine reported deaths nationally this year, eight of them confirmed by state officials. As of November 5, the CDC reported 5,182 cases in 47 states and jurisdictions and four deaths, though it is unclear which deaths it counted. Wisconsin officials noted that not everyone who falls ill is tested, so cases may go unreported.

How deaths are counted has become disputed. Ars Technica reports that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested Pennsylvania officials "fabricated" deaths and reportedly ordered the CDC to delete them; the outlet calls that suggestion false. The CDC now relies on federal death records, which take longer to process. Pennsylvania's health department told the outlet it has found no Franklin County cases meeting its criteria, though that investigation is open, even though the county coroner described a 39-year-old woman's death as possible measles complications. The page does not include a response from Kennedy or the CDC.

Next week, from November 10 to 13, a committee of infectious disease experts assembled by the Pan American Health Organization will review data from 2025 and early 2026 to assess whether measles has reestablished in the US. The country declared measles eliminated in 2000, and Ars Technica says that status is likely to be stripped.

Pope Leo XIV has arrived in South America for a 12-day, three-country trip, NPR reports. It is his longest trip yet and his first major overseas visit since surgery last month to remove the lower lobe of his right lung. Vatican officials say he has finished a two-week recovery and needs no further treatment. The Vatican's communications chief, Maria Montserrat Alvar, said his doctors are very confident and medical care will be on board.

The schedule includes 12 flights, 36 speeches and 10 cities, among them Cusco, Peru, at more than 11,000 feet, where altitude sickness is a risk. The first stop is Uruguay, which NPR describes as Latin America's most secular nation. Only about a third of Uruguayans identify as Catholic, according to pollster Mariana Pomiés. A proposed papal address to parliament drew a swift rebuke and was scrapped, but President Yamandú Orsi will oversee a welcome ceremony in Montevideo. Leo will also visit the Casavalle neighborhood on Saturday and say Mass in Florida on Sunday.

By Sunday he will be in Argentina, fulfilling a wish of Pope Francis, who never made the trip. NPR says the visit is an early test of how Leo addresses the Church's differences with right-wing populist leaders. It notes that President Javier Milei's austerity measures could put him at odds with a pope who has championed the poor, and that Milei's light-touch approach to AI regulation contrasts with Leo's call for ethical safeguards. The page does not include a response from Milei.
The trip ends in Peru, where Leo spent two decades and became a citizen in 2015. He will visit places where he lived and meet President Keiko Fujimori.

Police expect more women to come forward against Russell Brand, according to The Guardian. The Met Police commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said there could be "many more" victims. Sources told the paper that at least 10 other women are suspected of being attacked, and that the number may reach double digits. Rowley declined to confirm a figure, noting that some intelligence is third-hand and some suspected victims are reluctant to engage with the justice system.

Brand, 51, will be sentenced on Monday, with a lengthy jail term expected. He was convicted Thursday of raping a young fan at his London townhouse in 2009 and of sexually assaulting three women at a radio station, a recording studio and a bar. He was cleared of two further rape charges and one attempted indecent assault allegation. Victims are expected to describe the impact of his crimes in court on Monday.

The Met said Brand is under investigation over two further rape allegations, with files sent to specialist prosecutors. Next week, the team that built the case will begin sifting reports about other potential victims.

The trial prompted debate over rape myths after the defence asked women why they had not screamed. A No 10 source said Prime Minister Andy Burnham believes the victims' commissioner Claire Waxman's call for a legal duty on judges to direct juries on rape myths should be examined. The Ministry of Justice said judges can already give such directions and it will consider her proposals. Asked about a 2014 statement of support for Brand, Burnham said he had no idea of the full extent of what Brand did.

Israeli forces have closed the Ibrahimi Mosque in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron to Palestinian worshippers while thousands of Israeli settlers gather there for a Jewish religious observance, Al Jazeera reports. The Palestinian Ministry of Religious Endowments said worshippers and staff were barred from entering and the call to prayer was suspended. Mosque director Moataz Abu Sneineh told Al Jazeera that Israeli authorities intend to open the prayer halls and courtyards only to Israelis.

The closure began Friday afternoon and is set to last until 10pm Saturday. It coincides with an annual observance commemorating Sarah, wife of Abraham, who is traditionally believed to be buried at the site. Israeli troops also tightened checkpoints in Hebron's Old City, preventing some residents from entering or leaving their homes. Israeli forces told The Jerusalem Post they expected about 20,000 visitors, with hundreds of security personnel deployed. The page does not carry a separate Israeli government explanation of the closure.

The site is known to Jews as the Cave of the Patriarchs and is revered by Muslims and Jews as the burial place of Abraham and his family. Under a 1997 agreement between Israel and the Palestinian Authority, Israel holds security control over the Old City while the Palestinian municipality holds planning and construction powers. Al Jazeera says Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich announced in June a takeover of those powers, raising fears among Palestinians of exclusive Jewish use of the site.

The closure follows the end of a 10-day Israeli siege of Hebron, which Al Jazeera says involved hundreds of arrests, 15 home demolitions and the displacement of more than 3,300 Palestinians. The page also links to a separate report on settlers seizing eight homes in Jericho, but gives no details of it.

The Space Force, in partnership with the Pentagon's Golden Dome office, has chosen Viasat to build a Mission Operations Center for the Space Data Network Backbone, Breaking Defense reports. Space Systems Command said in a Thursday press release that Viasat received an indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity contract with a ceiling of $450 million to "design, field, and scale" the center. Viasat will act as network and mission system integration partner as the command expands its open-architecture ecosystem across several space-segment providers.

The backbone is a constellation of low Earth orbit satellites being built by SpaceX to provide high-speed, low-latency communications. According to Breaking Defense, it is meant to connect a broader network of military, and eventually commercial, sensor and communications satellites with decision-makers and weapons platforms. Its near-term focus is supporting the Trump administration's Golden Dome missile defense initiative.

The operations center will be the network's orchestration hub. Breaking Defense says such orchestration lets data shift automatically among constellations in different orbits and among ground stations, so traffic can move around bandwidth congestion or adversary jamming. The outlet likens the center to a software-run telephone exchange.

The release says the center will provide multi-vendor orchestration, multi-domain joint connectivity across air, land, sea and space, and real-time priority routing based on mission needs. Lt. Col. Alexa Eggert, materiel leader for the backbone program, said the center establishes the mission operations layer needed to integrate space data transport systems being developed across related efforts, and that bringing the systems together positions the Space Force to deliver a more integrated capability across multiple constellations.

Meta has added a feature called spaces to its Muse AI assistant, according to The Verge and TechCrunch. Spaces let users describe something in chat, such as a tracker, planner or project board, and have Muse build it. The Verge lists a shopping hub, school dashboard, music tracker and trivia game as examples. TechCrunch cites a holiday gift tracker, wedding planner and DIY project space.

The two outlets describe the feature a little differently. The Verge frames spaces as app-like experiences users can interact with directly by checking items off, adding notes and editing. TechCrunch's writer says that, as far as they can tell, spaces are essentially breakout conversations on a topic, which Meta calls custom experiences, where Muse works toward a goal for the user.

Both say spaces can connect to other apps. Meta says connected spaces keep themselves updated in the background, for example with new concert dates, price changes or savings progress. Users can pin spaces in the sidebar or main tab and schedule when they appear, such as showing a weekly planner during the workweek and weekend plans on Saturday. The Verge says spaces are rolling out to all Muse users, along with a specialized version of the Muse Wonder AI model, and that Meta is exploring ways to share and collaborate on spaces.

TechCrunch adds that Mark Zuckerberg said on X he has built a BBQ game, an event tracker and a home control dashboard. It also reports that Zuckerberg said in October that Muse agents had 10 million users in the US and Canada, and that Meta announced Muse Voice, for video chat and spoken commands, on Thursday.

Researchers have identified a three-way feedback loop that makes extreme heatwaves hotter than previously thought, according to New Scientist. The work, published in Science Advances, suggests that mid-latitude regions such as Europe face more intense heat than expected.

The study aims to explain why recent heatwaves have outstripped historical records and climate model predictions. In 2022 the UK exceeded 40°C for the first time, years earlier than predicted, and the 2021 Pacific Northwest heatwave also exceeded model projections. Scientists already knew that high-pressure systems let more solar radiation reach the surface, and that higher temperatures dry soils faster, removing the cooling effect of evaporation. The new finding is that at high enough temperatures, dry soil, high pressure and extreme heat reinforce one another, with dry soil helping to sustain high-pressure systems.

Lead researcher Kai Kornhuber of the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis said soils affected by circulation patterns then affect those patterns in return. His team found the feedback makes extreme heatwaves 10 per cent hotter than they would otherwise be, an effect not fully accounted for in model projections. He said that margin can separate a heatwave from a record-shattering one, with possible consequences for public health, transport and energy infrastructure, crops and ecosystems.

The article says Europe, Russia, North America, parts of South America and Australia will trigger the feedback more often as the world warms. Kornhuber said models need to include it properly. Dim Coumou of the Free University of Amsterdam, who was not described as part of the study, said the work solves part of the puzzle and shows models do not reproduce the mechanism well. He urged governments, including in Europe, to prepare for more intense heatwaves.

Brief bursts of vigorous everyday activity were linked to a markedly lower risk of dementia in a large study, New Scientist reports. People who accumulated about 3.7 minutes a day of vigorous routine movement, such as rushing for a bus, climbing stairs or carrying heavy shopping, had a 48 per cent lower dementia risk than sedentary people.

Nicholas Koemel at the University of Sydney and colleagues analysed data from 22,618 UK Biobank participants, mostly in their early 60s and free of dementia, who wore wrist accelerometers for seven days between 2013 and 2015. They were followed for around eight years, and 170 were diagnosed with dementia. Among people who did no exercise at all, 2.5 per cent developed dementia. The figure was 0.71 per cent among those who did not set aside exercise time but managed a few bouts of vigorous daily activity, and 0.59 per cent among those who also exercised deliberately. The activity was also associated with larger grey matter volumes in several brain regions and shrinking white matter hyperintensities.

The study is observational, so it cannot show that bursts of activity change dementia risk. Koemel said undiagnosed dementia could have left some people less able to be active. Mike Trott at the University of Queensland noted that the study captured only a week of activity, years before diagnoses. The findings are in a preprint.

The researchers speculate that short vigorous bursts may improve vascular health by lowering blood pressure and arterial stiffness. Koemel advised people to increase activity gradually, because sudden shifts could raise the risk of injury.
